title: Turning sermon videos into clips linked to Bible passages
subtitle: I did some of the logging work by hand, added the end point the logs were missing, and used AI agents to create the n8n pipeline that turns sermon videos into source-linked clips for a Bible-study app in development.

card.title: Turning sermon videos into source-linked clips
card.line: I had AI agents build and run the n8n pipeline, for a Bible-study app in development.

sections.headline: Turning sermon videos into clips linked to Bible passages
sections.subtext: Bibel TV's sermons, Bible studies and lectures are full of references to Bible verses, and the logs recorded where each reference started, never where it ended. I did some of the logging work by hand, added the end point, and used AI agents to create an n8n pipeline that turns timed transcripts into source-linked clips for a conversational AI Bible-study app in development.

sections.headline: Thousands of source-linked clips, from a pipeline nobody has to start

metrics.label: The setting
metrics.value: Bibel TV's catalog of sermons, Bible studies and lectures, and a conversational AI Bible-study app in development whose chat answers from sermon clips and from articles on gott-erklaert.de.

metrics.label: My part
metrics.value: I work single-handedly across the app's design, product management and development. I did some of the logging work by hand during onboarding, then created the n8n workflows with AI agents and live-tested, operated and iterated them.

metrics.label: What changed
metrics.value: Counted live on 9 October 2026: 11,405 sermon clips from 3,504 videos, and 3,574 transcripts processed (299 transcribed by the pipeline itself, the rest imported from the catalog's existing transcription). A pipeline result, not an adoption metric: the app is unpublished.

metrics.label: Three takeaways
metrics.value: Do the manual work before you automate it. Record where a reference ends as well as where it starts. Cut quoted text by code and let the model propose structure.

sections.headline: A relevant result that reads as irrelevant
sections.content:
Look up the creation account in the Bible feature, and a result appears titled "Who is Jesus?". The passage genuinely is discussed in that sermon. The title conceals it.

The search found the right source and still could not say why. An inherited title describes the parent video, not the reason this result surfaced.

sections.headline: A verse becomes an index into the whole catalog
sections.content:
The verse references power two features that run in opposite directions. From a video, you open the verse it cites. From a verse, you see which videos discuss it. The second direction is what turns a tagging job into a content graph.

It also makes the timestamp a product decision. A timecode is a jump target a viewer lands on, and landing mid-sentence is worse than not landing at all. If your product sits on hours of video, audio or archive material, this is where metadata stops being bookkeeping.

sections.headline: The logs knew where a verse came up, not where the passage ended
sections.content:
During onboarding I worked in the logging department and did some of the capture work on real videos myself. For every newly ingested video, someone watches it completely, captures its structure, timestamps each segment, screenshots graphics, extracts and documents the Bible verses, and picks a cover frame. The verse extraction alone took me three to five minutes per video, sometimes more. That is my own estimate from doing it, not a measurement.

The logs also had a structural gap. For each Bible reference they recorded a start time and nothing more: where a verse came up, not the span in which the sermon actually discussed it.

The goal was to automate the capture, with the existing logging as the starting point of the design, not its end state.

sections.headline: Adding the end point turned a mention into a clip
sections.content:
I added the end time: the span over which the video discusses the verse or passage. A reference stops being a point and becomes a segment.

A segment can carry its own metadata. I call it a virtual clip: a record over the original sermon, derived from transcript timestamps, not a newly rendered video file. It gets its own passage, summary and title instead of inheriting the sermon's. A sermon about Jesus that also talks about the creation story can carry a clip titled for what it says about creation.

sections.headline: Turn the transcript into product structure
sections.content: I created the workflows with AI agents rather than assembling them node by node, then live-tested, operated and iterated them in the product environment.

steps.label: Create one consistent transcript
steps.description: A transcription workflow obtains the source video, extracts the audio and stores the timed transcript segments in Postgres. The app's own catalog status decides whether a video has been transcribed by this pipeline, instead of accepting transcripts of unknown provenance.

steps.label: Take the fragile chain off the critical path
steps.description: The old route formatted HTML, copied files to S3, wrote transcripts back into the video platform and tracked them in a spreadsheet. I removed that chain from the critical path. The transcript now goes straight to the product database.

steps.label: Derive clips, chapters and topics
steps.description: A second workflow turns the timed transcript into Bible-passage clips, structural chapters and topics. Each clip's text is derived from the stored segments by code, not written by the model.

steps.label: Make each clip retrievable, and keep failure visible
steps.description: Embeddings and structured records connect each clip back to its source video and time range, so the app's chat can retrieve it. Model usage and estimated cost are recorded with the corpus data. Live n8n traces exposed an execution-order race and a broken upstream node reference; I corrected both and re-ran the workflow end to end.

images.alt: Pipeline in three stages. Every night, new transcripts are imported and their timed segments stored. Every 15 minutes, clips, chapters and topics are derived from the transcript segments. Each clip is made retrievable through embeddings and records that link it back to its source video and time range.
images.caption: Three stages, each linking its output back to the source video and time range.

images.alt: Sanitized overview of the real n8n sermon-insight workflow for an AI Bible study app, showing transcription inputs branching into Bible clip extraction, summaries, chapters, embeddings, topic classification and stored records.

sections.headline: The model proposes the structure; the quote is never the model's
sections.content:
The model proposes the Bible passage, the time range, the title and the summary. The time range has to come from the timestamps already in the transcript, not be invented. The quote under the transcript toggle is cut from the sermon's own transcript by code, so those words are the preacher's, never the model's.

Malformed clips are dropped, not published: no quote, no book, or an end before the start, and the parser filters them out.

images.alt: One clip open in the AI Bible study app, annotated. The time range (03:08), the title 'Nikodemus braucht neues Leben statt mehr Gesetzestreue', the summary and the passage Johannes 3,1-3 are labeled as model output. The transcript text under 'Transkript ausblenden' is labeled as cut from the transcript by code.

sections.headline: The corpus, counted, and the automation that keeps it current

metrics.label: Corpus
metrics.value: 11,405 sermon clips from 3,504 videos, 3,574 transcripts processed and 91 gott-erklärt articles, counted live on 9 October 2026

metrics.label: Automation
metrics.value: Every night, new transcripts are imported; every 15 minutes, a workflow turns them into clips, chapters and topics, without anyone starting a run

metrics.label: Product connection
metrics.value: The clips are available to the app's chat, which answers from clips and gott-erklärt articles only

metrics.label: Verified workflow
metrics.value: The corrected transcription path completed end to end; the sermon-insight workflow later passed a 31-node dry run on a real transcript

sections.narrative:
This is a pipeline result, not an adoption metric. The app is unpublished.

One attribution note: 3,275 of the 3,574 transcripts came from the catalog's existing transcription and were imported; 299 were transcribed by the pipeline itself. The clips, chapters, Bible-verse tagging and topics are the pipeline's own output.

sections.headline: Automation worth having shows its source and its seams
sections.content:
The useful automation is the one that keeps its source, its boundary and its failure state legible. A virtual clip points to a source video and a time range, and its quoted text comes from the same timed segments. The cost of each run is recorded with the data.

The order mattered to me as well. I did the capture work by hand before designing anything to replace it, so when someone asks how I know verse extraction takes minutes per video, the answer is that I did it.

sections.headline: In John 3, the clips carry their own titles
sections.content:
In the app's development build, John 3 shows a small marker after the verses that have clips. The passage lists them. A clip plays only its own window of the sermon, with its passage, its summary and a way back to the full video.

One of those clips comes from a sermon titled "Dem Gesetz gestorben (2/2)". Nothing in that title says John 3 or Nicodemus. The clip's own title does.

sections.headline: What carries over to your own catalog

steps.label: Do the manual work before you automate it.
steps.description: Long enough to know every step the task involves and where your time estimate comes from. If you can't say why it takes as long as it does, you aren't ready to replace it.

steps.label: Record where a reference ends as well as where it starts.
steps.description: A start point gives you a mention. A span gives the product something it can address, title and play. Check your own records for the half that's missing.

steps.label: Cut quoted text by code; let the model propose structure.
steps.description: Passages, ranges, titles and summaries are proposals you can check. Anything a reader would take as someone's words should come from the source, cut by code.

sections.headline: A catalog nobody has logged by hand needs that first
sections.content: If no one has ever logged your material manually, there is no baseline: no sense of what a unit of capture should be, no feel for where the judgment sits, and no honest estimate of what automation saves. Build the manual practice first, even lightly. And if your content has no natural unit smaller than the whole file, nothing like a passage, a scene or a topic, a clip has nothing to attach to.
Tell me where your catalog keeps a start time and no end, or which old chain still sits on the critical path of your content pipeline. Get in touch.
